claims.text: Self-service cafeteria with a wheat-heavy menu (wheat-noodle Ise udon and ramen, wheat-flour curry roux, battered/fried items); no information indicating gluten cross-contamination controls or a dedicated fryer.
Menu features soy-sauce ramen and Ise udon, both of which rely on standard wheat-containing soy sauce and wheat noodles.

The aquarium provides an ingredient list covering 28 major allergens (FY2026 PDF) and a low-allergen curry, but these are oriented toward school-group meals rather than individual celiac/vegan service.
A downloadable 28-allergen ingredient list is available, so diners can check specific dish components before ordering.
Fried shrimp and fried oyster set meals are signature dishes, indicating shared fryer use with wheat batter; no dedicated fryer is mentioned.
A seafood/izakaya menu (sashimi, set meals) where standard wheat-containing soy sauce is used; no gluten-free shoyu indicated.
Set meals include a complimentary Ise-lobster miso soup and the kitchen is built around fish and shellfish, so bonito/seafood dashi is pervasive.
Owner couple are known for warm, personal hospitality, which can make it easier to ask about ingredients face to face.

name: ごはんや ふくつぎ (Gohanya Fukutsugi)

claims.text: Core dishes are deep-fried (karaage, tonkatsu, miso katsu, ebi-fry) in wheat batter/breading, sharing a common fryer — high cross-contamination risk and no dedicated gluten-free fryer indicated.
Standard Japanese set-meal seasonings (soy sauce, miso, sauces) are used and almost certainly contain wheat; no wheat-free condiments documented.
Menu is meat- and seafood-based with miso-soup set meals; dashi almost certainly contains bonito/katsuo and no plant-based options are documented.

name: 本家かまどや 鳥羽店 (Honke Kamadoya Toba-ten)

claims.text: The chain's allergen notice states that factory and store production, cooking and plating are shared across products, so an item may pick up trace amounts of allergens (including wheat) not in its own recipe.
Tempura items in some bento are all cooked in a common batter: 一部のお弁当に使用している天ぷらは、全ての食材を共通の天ぷら衣で調理しています。

The chain notes the common view that wheat allergen is broken down during soy-sauce brewing, so soy sauce need not necessarily be removed for wheat allergy — but this does not make a dish certified gluten-free for celiac diners.
のり, ちりめんじゃこ and あおさ used in some bento are harvested by methods that also catch shrimp and crab (えび・かに が混ざる漁法), indicating shellfish/animal cross-contact in seemingly plant items.
The chain publishes a per-item allergen search and an 8-allergen disclosure (小麦・そば・卵・乳・落花生・えび・かに・くるみ) and advises confirming current information, as allergen/nutrition data is updated periodically.
Base is white rice using selected domestic rice, and the menu allows swapping the rice and choosing components, giving a careful diner room to build a simpler box.
A published online allergen lookup tool exists, so ingredients can be checked per item before ordering.

name: 居酒屋味のやまもと (Izakaya Aji no Yamamoto)

claims.text: Tempura (shrimp and chikuwa) is on the menu, so wheat batter is fried in the kitchen; no dedicated gluten-free fryer is indicated.
As a traditional izakaya, sashimi and dishes are served with standard (wheat-containing) soy sauce; no gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned.
Seafood-focused kitchen where bonito/kombu dashi and fish are used throughout; assume hidden fish stock in seasoned dishes.
Sashimi and seafood are sourced fresh from the local market, and the owner-operator is hands-on, which can make direct dietary conversation easier.
Tempura and fried items (e.g. fried shrimp) share fry oil with wheat-battered foods, a cross-contamination risk for celiacs.
Sashimi and seafood rice bowls are served with standard soy sauce, which typically contains wheat; no wheat-free/tamari alternative is advertised.
The kitchen is centered on raw fish and shellfish, and dashi/seasonings likely contain bonito or other fish; plant-only preparation is not assured.

name: 海鮮茶屋えびしま (Kaisen Chaya Ebishima)

claims.text: Menu includes fried items (squid fries in the shio-sai bowl) and grilled seafood sets; no dedicated fryer or allergen separation is documented, so wheat cross-contact should be assumed.
Core dishes — sashimi, kaisen-don, negitoro-don and the local てこね寿司 — rely on soy sauce / soy-based marinades, which in Japan are typically brewed with wheat.
Entirely a seafood kitchen; rice and soup items would be prepared with fish-based dashi and there are no vegan dishes.
Menu includes Ise udon (wheat noodles) and likely fried/tempura items, so shared kitchen surfaces and frying oil are a cross-contamination risk; no GF handling is indicated.
As a Japanese seafood restaurant, standard soy sauce (which typically contains wheat) is expected for dipping and seasoning; no wheat-free shoyu is advertised.
Seafood-only menu built on fish, shellfish and bonito-based dashi; no plant-based dishes are offered.
Core offerings are grilled and raw Ise Bay shellfish (lobster, abalone, sazae, clams, oysters) that are naturally wheat-free in their unseasoned form.
